title: What are the ways to read a very large text file in Java and their trade-offs — `Scanner` is slow (avoid for big files); `BufferedReader.readLine()` is the simple memory-friendly baseline; `Files.lines(path)` gives a lazy, streaming `Stream<String>` (must be closed — it holds a file handle); low-level `FileChannel` + `ByteBuffer` or a `MappedByteBuffer` (memory-mapped) are fastest for huge files but require manual byte→text handling — and what is the ONE rule that matters most regardless of API (STREAM/process line-by-line or in bounded chunks, never load the whole file into a `List`/`String` in memory, or you risk an `OutOfMemoryError`)?
shortTitle: What are the ways to read a very large text file in Java, and their trade-offs?

s1_definition.profdef: Reading a very large text file in Java is about choosing an API whose memory footprint stays bounded regardless of file size. `Scanner` is convenient but slow because of its parsing and regex overhead, so it is a poor fit for big files. `BufferedReader.readLine()` is the simple, memory-friendly baseline that reads one line at a time through a reusable buffer. `Files.lines(path)` returns a lazy `Stream<String>` that reads lines on demand and must be closed because it holds an open file handle. For the highest throughput on huge files, `FileChannel` with a `ByteBuffer`, or a memory-mapped `MappedByteBuffer`, reads raw bytes fastest but forces you to handle byte-to-text decoding and line splitting yourself. The one rule that dominates all of them is to process line by line or in bounded chunks and never load the entire file into a single `List` or `String`, or you risk an `OutOfMemoryError`.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India must process a transaction file with a hundred million lines. Trying to read the whole file into memory at once is like trying to carry every ledger book in the archive in your arms at the same time — you will collapse (an out-of-memory crash). The right habit is to carry and process one book at a time, put it down, then pick up the next. `Scanner` is a very careful but slow clerk who inspects every word. `BufferedReader` is a steady clerk who hands you one line at a time. `Files.lines` is a conveyor belt that delivers lines on demand but you must switch the belt off when done. `FileChannel` and memory mapping are a forklift moving raw pallets — fastest for huge loads, but you must unpack the pallets into readable pages yourself.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick BufferedReader or Files.lines for simple streaming, FileChannel or mapping for maximum speed, but above all stream line-by-line or in bounded chunks and never load the whole file into memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reading a very large text file in Java is about choosing an API whose memory footprint stays bounded regardless of file size. `Scanner` is convenient but slow because of its parsing and regex overhead, so it is a poor fit for big files. `BufferedReader.readLine()` is the simple, memory-friendly baseline that reads one line at a time through a reusable buffer. `Files.lines(path)` returns a lazy `Stream<String>` that reads lines on demand and must be closed because it holds an open file handle. For the highest throughput on huge files, `FileChannel` with a `ByteBuffer`, or a memory-mapped `MappedByteBuffer`, reads raw bytes fastest but forces you to handle byte-to-text decoding and line splitting yourself. The one rule that dominates all of them is to process line by line or in bounded chunks and never load the entire file into a single `List` or `String`, or you risk an `OutOfMemoryError`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India must process a transaction file with a hundred million lines. Trying to read the whole file into memory at once is like trying to carry every ledger book in the archive in your arms at the same time — you will collapse (an out-of-memory crash). The right habit is to carry and process one book at a time, put it down, then pick up the next. `Scanner` is a very careful but slow clerk who inspects every word. `BufferedReader` is a steady clerk who hands you one line at a time. `Files.lines` is a conveyor belt that delivers lines on demand but you must switch the belt off when done. `FileChannel` and memory mapping are a forklift moving raw pallets — fastest for huge loads, but you must unpack the pallets into readable pages yourself.

**One line to remember:** Pick BufferedReader or Files.lines for simple streaming, FileChannel or mapping for maximum speed, but above all stream line-by-line or in bounded chunks and never load the whole file into memory.

sections.s2_technical:
The central danger with large files is memory. If you call `Files.readAllLines(path)` or `Files.readString(path)`, the entire file is pulled into a `List<String>` or a single `String` on the heap. For a few kilobytes that is fine; for a multi-gigabyte transaction log it throws `OutOfMemoryError`. So every good approach keeps only a small, bounded amount of the file in memory at any instant.

`Scanner` wraps a stream and offers `hasNextLine` and `nextLine`, plus token parsing like `nextInt`. It is pleasant for small inputs but slow for big files because it synchronizes, compiles and applies regular expressions for delimiters, and does extra parsing work per token. For reading millions of lines you feel this overhead sharply, so the guidance is to avoid `Scanner` for large files.

`BufferedReader.readLine()` is the classic memory-friendly baseline. You wrap a `FileReader` or an `InputStreamReader` with a specified charset in a `BufferedReader`, and the buffer reads a block of bytes at a time while `readLine` hands you one line per call. Only the current line plus the internal buffer are in memory, so footprint is tiny and constant no matter how large the file is. It is fast, explicit, and easy to reason about, which is why it remains the default for line-oriented processing.

`Files.lines(path)` returns a `Stream<String>` that reads lines lazily as the stream is consumed, so it combines the bounded memory of `readLine` with the expressiveness of the Streams API — you can `filter`, `map`, and `collect` per line. The critical caveat is that this stream is backed by an open file, so it must be closed, which means using it in a try-with-resources block. Forgetting to close it leaks a file handle, and under load you exhaust the operating system's handle limit. Also, terminal operations like `collect(toList())` on it will still blow memory if you collect the whole file, so you must keep the pipeline streaming or reduce to a bounded result such as a count or a sum.

For the highest throughput on truly huge files, you drop to the channel level. `FileChannel.read(ByteBuffer)` reads a block of raw bytes into a reusable buffer; you decode those bytes to characters with a `CharsetDecoder` and split on line boundaries yourself, refilling the buffer as you consume it. A memory-mapped `MappedByteBuffer` from `FileChannel.map` goes further, mapping file pages into memory so the OS pages data in on demand with no per-read system call and no copy. These are the fastest options, but they are low level: you must handle character encoding, multi-byte characters that straddle buffer boundaries, and line splitting manually, which is error-prone. You reach for them only when profiling shows the simpler APIs are the bottleneck.

A few senior nuances. Always specify the charset explicitly, for example `StandardCharsets.UTF_8`, rather than relying on the platform default, which differs across machines and can corrupt data. If the work per line is heavy and independent, you can parallelize, but beware that `Files.lines().parallel()` splits poorly on unindexed text and often does not help; a better pattern is to read sequentially and dispatch line batches to a thread pool. For fixed-width or binary-ish records, channels and mapping shine because you can address records by offset. And for append-and-tail scenarios, a channel with positional reads is the right tool.

The one rule that matters most, regardless of API, is this: process the file incrementally. Stream line by line, or read bounded chunks, and reduce to a bounded result as you go. Never accumulate the whole file into a `List`, a `StringBuilder`, or a `String`, because that makes your memory grow with file size and guarantees an `OutOfMemoryError` on a large enough input. The API is a performance choice; the streaming discipline is a correctness requirement.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India receives a daily transaction file with tens of millions of lines, each line holding an account id and an amount. A developer first wrote `Files.readAllLines(path)` and summed the list; it worked in testing on a small sample but crashed with `OutOfMemoryError` on the real file. This is the one rule in action: never load the whole file; stream it.

Problem 2 — The team needed to total the amount credited to Rajesh's account across the whole file without ever holding more than one line in memory. This is the `BufferedReader.readLine()` baseline and the `Files.lines` streaming case: read line by line and keep only a running `BigDecimal` total.

Problem 3 — Someone used `Files.lines(path)` but forgot to close it in a loop that ran per file, and the service eventually failed with too many open files. This is the must-close caveat: `Files.lines` holds a file handle and must live in try-with-resources.

The mini-project processes a large transaction file three ways to compare them: the memory-friendly `BufferedReader` baseline, the lazy `Files.lines` stream closed properly, and a note on the channel approach for maximum speed. Each computes the total credited to Rajesh (SAV2001) while keeping memory bounded. We generate a sample file, then process it.

The code contains: a `TransactionFileProcessor` with a `readLine`-based method and a `Files.lines`-based method; and a runnable demo that creates a sample file and runs both, proving bounded memory.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
javac -d out $(find src -name "*.java")

# Run with a SMALL heap to prove the streaming approach stays bounded
java -Xmx64m -cp out com.bank.largefile.LargeFileDemo

# A readAllLines version on a real multi-GB file would die with:

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a transaction file where SAV2001 appears 100000 times with Rs.100.00 each and CUR3001 appears 100000 times with Rs.250.00 each. We want the total credited to SAV2001.

Step 1: The demo writes the file line by line using a `BufferedWriter`, so even creating the file never holds it all in memory.

Step 2: `totalForAccountViaReader` opens a `BufferedReader` with UTF-8. The reader fills an internal buffer with a block of bytes; `readLine` hands back one line. Only that single line plus the buffer exist in memory.

Step 3: For each line, we check if it starts with SAV2001 and, if so, parse the amount and add it to a running `BigDecimal total`. After the loop, total is 100000 times Rs.100.00 equals Rs.10000000.00. Memory stayed flat the entire time.

Step 4: `totalForAccountViaStream` opens `Files.lines` inside try-with-resources. The stream reads lines lazily; `filter` keeps SAV2001 lines, `map` parses the amount, and `reduce` sums them into a single `BigDecimal`. The result is bounded — we never collect the lines into a list.

Step 5: The try-with-resources block closes the stream, releasing the file handle. If we had forgotten this in a long-running service processing many files, we would eventually hit too many open files.

Step 6: Both methods produce Rs.10000000.00, and the whole run fits in a 64-megabyte heap, proving the streaming discipline, not the API choice, is what keeps us safe.

Oct 26, 2026 3:46:50 PM com.bank.largefile.LargeFileDemo main
INFO: Files.lines  total for SAV2001: Rs.10000000.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:50 PM com.bank.largefile.LargeFileDemo main

```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  transactions.csv  (200,000 lines — far bigger in production)
    │
    ├─ WRONG PATH ───────────────────┐   ├─ RIGHT PATH ──────────────────┐
    │  Files.readAllLines(path)       │   │  BufferedReader.readLine()     │
    │  → List<String> of ALL lines    │   │  → one line in memory at a time│
    │  → heap grows with file size    │   │  → constant footprint          │
    │  → OutOfMemoryError           │   │  → running BigDecimal total    │
    └──────────────────────────────────┘   └────────────────────────────────┘
                                             │
                                             ▼
   Files.lines(path)  [try-with-resources]   lazy Stream<String>
     │ filter(startsWith "SAV2001,")
     │ map(parse amount → BigDecimal)
     │ reduce(ZERO, add)               ← BOUNDED result, not a collected List
     ▼
   total = 100,000 × Rs.100.00 = Rs.10,000,000.00
     │
     ▼
   stream.close()  ← releases file handle (else: too many open files)

   FASTEST (huge files): FileChannel + ByteBuffer / MappedByteBuffer
     → raw bytes → CharsetDecoder → split '\n' yourself (low-level, manual)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
There are several ways to read a very large text file in Java, and I pick among them by weighing speed against simplicity, but they all share one non-negotiable rule. Scanner is convenient but slow for big files because of its synchronization and regular-expression parsing, so I avoid it there. BufferedReader with readLine is my simple, memory-friendly baseline, because it keeps only the current line and a small buffer in memory, so the footprint is constant no matter how big the file is. Files dot lines gives me a lazy stream of lines that reads on demand and lets me filter, map, and reduce expressively, but it holds an open file handle, so I always use it inside try-with-resources or I will leak handles and eventually hit a too-many-open-files error. When I truly need maximum throughput on a huge file, I drop to FileChannel with a ByteBuffer, or a memory-mapped MappedByteBuffer, which are the fastest because the operating system pages data in with no per-read system call and no copy, but they force me to decode bytes to text and split lines myself, including multi-byte characters that straddle buffer boundaries, so I only reach for them when profiling proves the simpler APIs are the bottleneck.

The one rule that matters most, no matter which API I choose, is to process the file incrementally, line by line or in bounded chunks, and to reduce to a bounded result as I go. I never load the whole file into a list or a single string with readAllLines or readString, because then my memory grows with the file and a large enough file guarantees an out-of-memory error.

In my work at National Bank of India this came up with a daily transaction file of tens of millions of lines. A colleague's first version used readAllLines and summed the list, which passed on a small sample and then crashed in production with an out-of-memory error. I rewrote it to stream with BufferedReader, keeping only a running BigDecimal total per account, and it ran comfortably in a tiny heap. For the more expressive reporting jobs I used Files dot lines inside try-with-resources, reducing to a single total rather than collecting the lines. The lesson I always repeat is that the API is a performance decision, but streaming is a correctness requirement.
